claims.text: RFC 9309 describes a robots.txt file as groups that start with one or more user-agent lines followed by zero or more allow or disallow rules; if the last group has no rules, it implicitly allows everything.
acceptable_patterns: groups? start(?:s)? with one or more user-agent lines
followed by zero or more (?:allow|disallow) rules

claims.text: For user-agent selection, matching is case-insensitive against the crawler product token; if multiple groups match, their rules are combined, and if no specific group matches, the user-agent: * group is used if present, otherwise no rules apply.

Allow and disallow rules are matched against the URI path from the first octet, the most specific match is the one with the greatest number of matching octets, and if equivalent allow and disallow rules conflict, allow should be used.
If no rule matches, or the applicable group has no rules, the URI is allowed, and /robots.txt is implicitly allowed.

For percent encoding, octets outside ASCII and octets in the reserved range are percent-encoded before comparison; percent-encoded ASCII octets in the URI are decoded before comparison except when the octet is a reserved URI character or outside the unreserved range.

RFC 9309 treats an unavailable robots.txt as a fetch where the server indicates the resource is unavailable; in HTTP the answer cites 4xx as the example range, and in that case the crawler may access any resource on the server.
acceptable_patterns: may access any resource on the server

claims.text: If redirects exceed five consecutive hops, the crawler may treat robots.txt as unavailable.

The cited answer separately says unreachable robots.txt, such as server or network failure with HTTP 5xx as the example range, requires the crawler to assume complete disallow, though after a reasonably long time it may instead treat the file as unavailable or use a cached copy.

rejected_claims.text: Allow always overrides disallow in RFC 9309.
rejected_claims.reason: Contradicted by the supplied answer, which says longest-path specificity decides first and allow only breaks ties between equivalent rules.

rejected_claims.text: RFC 9309 requires path matching to be case-sensitive.
rejected_claims.reason: Contradicted by the supplied answer, which says path matching SHOULD be case sensitive, not MUST.
